steps.user_message: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm head of household in Chicago IL. My W-2 from Riverside Hospital shows $64,800. I had $15,000 in 1099 income (IT contracting, 6 clients), $1,560 from Goldman Sachs Marcus, and $290 from Charles Schwab. I have a home office (130 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $2,400/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $3,600 (Navient, 2017–2019). I donated $1,400 to Habitat for Humanity with receipt, and had $890 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Short answer up front
- You should almost certainly take the standard deduction for 2023 (Head of Household = $20,800). Your known itemizable amounts (charity $1,400, no mortgage interest reported, SALT unknown) are far below the standard deduction.
- Still claim several important deductions on your tax return that are independent of itemizing: home‑office and other business expenses on Schedule C (for your 1099 contracting), deduction for one‑half of self‑employment tax (Schedule SE), the student‑loan interest adjustment (up to $2,500, subject to phaseout), and possibly the 20% QBI deduction.
- Forms you will need (federal): Form 1040, Schedule 1 (adjustments), Schedule C (business), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), Schedule B (interest over $1,500), and Form 8995 (QBI) if you claim the QBI deduction. For Illinois: IL‑1040.

Details and numbers (approximate)
1) Income to report
- W‑2 wages: $64,800 (report on Form 1040)
- 1099 self‑employment (IT contracting): $15,000 (report on Schedule C)
- Interest: $1,560 (Goldman Sachs Marcus) + $290 (Charles Schwab) = $1,850 (report; because total interest > $1,500 you must file Schedule B)

2) Business (Schedule C) deductions you can/should claim
- Home office: you have exclusive use of 130 sq ft of a 620 sq ft apartment → business % = 130/620 ≈ 21.0%.
  - If you use the actual method, you can allocate 21% of allowable home expenses to the business (rent is $2,400/month = $28,800/year → rent share ≈ $28,800 × 0.21 ≈ $6,038). (You can also include utilities if you pay them and allocate the same percentage.)
  - Alternatively, the simplified method would be 130 sq ft × $5 = $650. The actual method gives a much larger deduction here because your rent is high.
- Other business expenses: the $890 in work expenses (assuming they are ordinary and necessary for your contracting) are deductible on Schedule C.
- These reduce your Schedule C profit and therefore reduce both income tax and self‑employment tax.

3) Self‑employment tax
- You will owe self‑employment tax on your net self‑employment earnings (Schedule SE). You may deduct one‑half of the self‑employment tax as an adjustment on Schedule 1 (this reduces AGI).

4) Student loan interest
- You paid $3,600 in student loan interest (Navient). The maximum student loan interest adjustment is $2,500. Whether you get the full $2,500 is subject to the MAGI phaseout: for single/head of household the 2023 phaseout is $75,000–$90,000.
- Rough estimate using the numbers above (and including the big home‑office rent allocation on Schedule C) puts your MAGI below $75k, so you’re likely eligible for the full $2,500 student‑loan interest deduction. If your MAGI ends up between $75k and $90k there will be a partial deduction; above $90k you get none.

5) Charitable contribution
- Your $1,400 donation to Habitat for Humanity is an itemized deduction (Schedule A). Because the HOH standard deduction is $20,800, that $1,400 alone is far less than standard; unless you have large state/local tax, mortgage interest, or medical expenses you will not beat the standard deduction.

6) Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction
- You may be eligible for the 20% QBI deduction (Form 8995) on your qualified business income from the contracting work. With a small net profit (example ~ $8k), the QBI deduction will be modest (about 20% of your qualified net business income), but it still reduces taxable income.

Approximate walkthrough (illustrative)
- Gross income: 64,800 (W2) + 15,000 (1099) + 1,850 (interest) = 81,650
- Example Schedule C net after home‑office rent allocation (~$6,038) + $890 other expenses → net ≈ $8,072
- Self‑employment tax (approx) ≈ $1,140 → half deductible ≈ $570
- AGI before student loan interest ≈ 64,800 + 8,072 + 1,850 − 570 ≈ 74,150
- Student loan interest deduction: you can likely take $2,500 (maximum) → AGI after ≈ 71,650
- Standard deduction (HOH) = 20,800 → taxable income before QBI ≈ 50,850
- QBI deduction (~20% of $8,072 ≈ $1,614) would reduce taxable income further.

Because your itemizable deductions are low relative to the HOH standard deduction, you’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction and still claim the business‑related deductions on Schedule C, the SE tax deduction, and the student loan interest above the line.

Forms and documents to gather
- W‑2 from Riverside Hospital
- All 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC for the 6 contracting clients (report all 1099 income on Schedule C)
- 1099‑INT statements from Goldman Sachs Marcus and Charles Schwab
- Records/receipts for home office: floor plan, proof of exclusive use, rent receipts/lease, utility bills (if you’ll use actual method)
- Receipts/records for the $890 work expenses (invoices, receipts)
- Student loan interest statement (Form 1098‑E) from Navient
- Charitable donation receipt from Habitat for Humanity
- Any state tax withheld info (from W‑2) for IL return

State filing (Illinois)
- You must file IL‑1040 for Illinois. Illinois starts from your federal AGI; interest is taxable by IL. Include the same income amounts on your IL return as required. (If you paid substantial state/local taxes and are thinking itemizing on federal to capture SALT, remember federal SALT deduction is capped at $10,000.)

Other practical notes and recommendations
- Keep careful documentation for the home office deduction (exclusive use, measurement, lease/rent payments); the IRS is stricter about home office claims.
- The home office and other business deductions are reported on Schedule C and reduce both income and self‑employment tax. They do not require you to itemize on Schedule A.
- Because you have self‑employment income, plan for estimated tax payments for 2024 (quarterly) if this contracting continues.
- If you want, I can:
  - Produce a simple worksheet with the numbers above updated to any additional amounts you provide (state tax withheld, utilities, any other deductible expenses).
  - Draft a checklist of documents for your tax preparer or for filing software.
  - Estimate your federal tax liability given the numbers above.

Caveat
- This is general guidance and approximations. Exact phaseout amounts, taxable income, and allowable deductions depend on full details (any retirement contributions, other income, exact utility amounts, state withholding, and other adjustments). If you want an exact tax calculation or are concerned about audit exposure for a large home‑office rent allocation, consider working with a CPA or tax preparer.

Do you want me to run a more precise estimate of your federal tax (I can use the exact numbers you give for utilities, state tax withheld, retirement contributions, and any other expenses), or prepare a document listing the forms and a folder checklist for your tax preparer?
